parts.given_text: For a roughly spherical mass distribution, circular-orbit speed obeys v² = GM(<r)/r. Use this supplied relation to interpret the rotation curve.

answer.text: Official answer A; editorial worked explanation: The horizontal variable d is measured from Earth’s surface, so the distance from Earth’s centre is r=R+d. Outside Earth, V=−GM/(R+d). At d=0, V is finite and negative, −GM/R; as d increases it rises toward zero with a decreasing positive gradient. Option A has this behaviour. A graph proportional to −1/d would incorrectly diverge at the surface and corresponds to option B’s shape.
answer.evidence: Official May 2025 Physics HL Paper 1A TZ1 markscheme 2225-6707M, PDF page 3; editorial explanation independently checked against the complete original source question.

answer.text:
Official answer checked; editorial worked explanation:

The free-body diagram has two radial forces: gravitational force GMm/R² directed inward toward the asteroid centre, and normal force N directed outward. The inward gravitational arrow must be longer because their difference supplies the inward centripetal force; there is no separate “centripetal force” arrow. Taking inward as positive, GMm/R² − N = mω²R, so N = m(GM/R² − ω²R).

parts.label: b

answer.text: Official markscheme inequality; editorial worked explanation: From part (a), N=m(GM/R²−ω²R). Contact requires N≥0. Therefore GM/R²−ω²R≥0, so ω²≤GM/R³ and ω≤√(GM/R³). At the limiting angular speed N=0; a larger angular speed would require an impossible inward normal force from the surface.
answer.evidence: Official May 2024 Physics HL Paper 2 TZ2 markscheme 2224-6708M, PDF page 12; editorial explanation independently recalculated from the source.

parts.given_text: Use the checked result from part (a): N=m(GM/R²−ω²R).

answer.text:
Official answer checked; editorial worked explanation:

Radiation intensity follows the inverse-square law. At four times Earth’s distance, I = 1360/(4²) = 85.0 W m⁻², which confirms the stated value.

parts.label: c.ii

answer.text:
Official answer checked; editorial worked explanation:

Under the source answer’s equal absorbing-area and emitting-area assumption, equilibrium gives 85 = σT⁴. Thus T = (85/(5.67 × 10⁻⁸))^(1/4) = 197 K, about 2.0 × 10² K. If the probe is instead an isothermal sphere that absorbs over πR² and emits over 4πR², then σT⁴ = 85/4 and T = 139 K, about 140 K; the official markscheme accepts this alternative.

parts.given_text: Checked result from the preceding source part: incident solar intensity at the probe is 85 W m⁻². State a geometry assumption for the absorbing and emitting areas.

answer.text: Official markscheme conclusion: the projectile does not escape; editorial worked explanation: At the surface, gravitational potential energy is −GMm/R. With initial kinetic energy 2GMm/(3R), the total energy is E=2GMm/(3R)−GMm/R=−GMm/(3R). Escape to infinity requires total energy at least zero, so this negative-energy trajectory remains bound.
answer.evidence: Official May 2024 Physics HL Paper 2 TZ2 markscheme 2224-6708M, PDF page 15; editorial explanation independently recalculated from the source.

answer.text: Official markscheme result 0.52 N kg⁻¹; editorial worked explanation: E₀ is at r=R and E₁ is at r=3R/2, so their radial separation is Δr=R/2=(8.5×10⁶)/2=4.25×10⁶ m. Estimating the average field by |g|≈|ΔV|/Δr gives (2.2×10⁶)/(4.25×10⁶)=0.518 N kg⁻¹≈0.52 N kg⁻¹.
answer.evidence: Official May 2024 Physics HL Paper 2 TZ2 markscheme 2224-6708M, PDF page 15; editorial explanation independently recalculated from the source.

answer.text: Official markscheme result: E₂ is a concentric circle of radius 3R; editorial worked explanation: V(r)=−GM/r. Since V(E₁)−V(E₀)=GM/(3R)=2.2×10⁶ J kg⁻¹, another equal outward increase requires V(E₂)=−GM/(3R). Therefore r₂=3R. Draw E₂ outside E₁, centred on P, with twice E₁'s radius.

notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

Potential is a scalar, so add its contributions algebraically. Use mgΔh only for a small height change where g is approximately uniform.

ibd-59d51577e3fd9550-q25:whole.hint: Replace the centre-distance r in V=−GM/r by R+d before comparing the intercept and asymptote.
notes: Gravitational potential is defined as zero at infinity, so its value at every finite exterior distance is negative.
Because d starts at the surface, d=0 still corresponds to a nonzero centre-distance R and a finite potential.

ibd-641ca00f2c84853d-q24:whole.hint: Draw the direction towards each attracting mass and measure distances from the centres of the masses.
notes: Outside a spherical mass, g = GM/r² and F = mg. Add field contributions as vectors when more than one mass is present.
An altitude above a surface is not the radius in the formula: r = R + h. The test mass affects force but not the field strength at its position.

ibd-641ca00f2c84853d-q25:whole.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

fast-duplicate-production-002-a-5-a.hint: Draw only the real radial interactions on the probe, then set their inward resultant equal to mω²R.
notes: The inward gravitational-force arrow must be longer than the outward normal-force arrow for this circular motion.
Centripetal force is the resultant of the real forces; adding it as a third force would double-count the resultant.

ibd-996809f014b31dce-q5:b.hint: Use the supplied normal-force expression and impose the physical contact condition N≥0; equality gives the limiting angular speed.
notes: A surface can push the probe outward but cannot pull it inward, so the calculated normal force cannot be negative.
At the contact limit gravity alone supplies the required centripetal force, giving ω_max=√(GM/R³).

fast-duplicate-production-002-a-5-b-i.hint: Apply inverse-square scaling to the solar constant using the factor-four increase in distance.
notes: The distance factor must be squared, so four times farther means one sixteenth of the intensity.
The solar constant is the reference intensity at Earth’s orbital distance from the Sun.

fast-duplicate-production-002-a-5-b-ii.hint: Choose a geometry model, write its absorbed-emitted power balance, and use the corresponding area ratio consistently.
notes: The 197 K result assumes the same effective area absorbs the incident intensity and emits black-body radiation.
The isothermal-sphere model has projected absorption area πR² and emission area 4πR², giving the accepted 140 K alternative.

ibd-996809f014b31dce-q8:a.hint: Set gravitational potential energy to zero at infinity and test the sign of the projectile's total mechanical energy at launch.
notes: The given kinetic energy has coefficient 2/3; reversing that fraction changes the physical conclusion.
Zero total energy is the threshold for escape with zero speed at infinity. A negative total energy means the projectile is gravitationally bound.

ibd-996809f014b31dce-q8:b.i.hint: Find the radial spacing between E₀ and E₁, then use field strength as the potential gradient magnitude.
notes: Gravitational potential difference has units J kg⁻¹; dividing by metres gives N kg⁻¹.
This is an average-field estimate across a finite interval because the field varies with radius.

ibd-996809f014b31dce-q8:b.ii.hint: Write V=−GM/r at E₀ and E₁, then add the same potential increase once more to find the radius of E₂.
notes: Equal potential intervals do not correspond to equal radial intervals because V varies as −1/r.
E₁ has radius 3R/2 and E₂ has radius 3R, so the new circle is concentric and twice E₁'s radius.

ibd-1c0b8836869c8bdf-q21:whole.hint: For a circular orbit, gravity supplies the inward acceleration. Use the radius measured from the central body’s centre.
notes: Equating GMm/r² = mv²/r gives v = √(GM/r), then T = 2πr/v. This leads to T² proportional to r³.
Orbiting objects are in free fall, not outside gravity. A geostationary orbit must also be equatorial, prograde and have Earth’s rotation period.

ibd-a4aeacaa02d5bc2c-q33:whole.hint: Compare the starting total mechanical energy with the minimum needed to reach infinity.
notes: With zero potential at infinity, the minimum escape condition is ½mv_e² − GMm/R = 0, so v_e = √(2GM/R).
Escape speed is different from circular orbital speed at the same radius. For ratios, use √(M/R); the escaping object’s mass cancels.
